# Tasks and subtasks

## Create a clear task

Use one accountable owner per released task. Start every actionable task and subtask title with a verb, without number prefixes. Native section headings are exempt. Make the title understandable in My Tasks, such as “Test the booking form and record the result.” Put the task in the correct project and section. Keep it unassigned during preparation.

Write the expected result, purpose, exact work, source links, limits, output destination, relevant timing, completion checks, and reviewer/approval requirements. Start main-task descriptions with the Deliverables block from the brief formats: each named output has a working link, final link, and required proof. Pending final links are filled as work is produced. Link reusable SOPs rather than pasting long general instructions, but include enough context to start without reconstructing chat history.

For a small job, a short Action / Reference / Done when / Save here format is enough. Remove missing-input placeholders before release; leave not-yet-produced output links clearly marked pending.

## Choose useful subtasks

Start with the main task's outcome. Each subtask represents one independently finishable result or meaningful work step with an observable done condition. Include each required action once. Split separate graphics when they have different inputs, outputs, reviews, or proof; do not hide that work inside 'Do graphics'. A coherent batch sharing inputs and one review can stay together. Do not turn each mouse click into a subtask. Use a subtask when ownership, timing, discussion, proof, or review needs separate tracking. Tiny checks with the same owner and timing can remain checklist items.

Open the main task, add a subtask with a verb-first, unnumbered title, leave it unassigned, and fill its inputs, action, destination, completion check, and wait conditions. Make it understandable when opened directly from My Tasks. Add relevant dates and real dependencies. Verify its main-task relationship and actual display position. Write at about Grade 8, no higher than Grade 9–10, using the communication skill. A brief may link sources but must not require reconstructing the main task or chat history.

Keep nesting shallow. If work becomes independently managed, consider a separate main task or project while preserving links and history. Counts alone do not decide the structure.

## Set visible working order

Determine the intended order before building. Use the exposed placement controls with exact section and neighboring task IDs where supported. Do not assume creation order, title prefixes, dates, or dependencies set the displayed sequence. Read all pages of the relevant section/task/subtask lists; correct reversed or misplaced items and read again. When the API cannot establish the displayed order, use an authorized visible check or report verification unavailable; do not claim it passed.

For repeated assignments, prove one complete unassigned worker path before copying it. A matching count is insufficient.

## Create real subtask sections

For multi-stage lists, use native subtask section dividers such as Prepare, Produce, Review and correct, Deliver. Match these names and their order to the main description.

In Asana's web interface, focus inside the subtask list and use Tab + N. Verify the divider appears inside that main task, and the action subtasks sit beneath the intended divider. Through tools, use a verified supported native-section operation; a tool called “create section” may support only project sections, so inspect its schema and read the result back.

Never fake a section with an ordinary task titled “SECTION — Research,” an unassigned heading task, or an extra nesting level. If native subtask sections are required and unsupported, stop that setup step and report the missing capability. Keep actual subtasks correctly attached.

## Ownership, visibility, and shared tasks

A worker's section does not assign its tasks. After the full release batch passes, assign each actionable main task and subtask, then read every assignee back. Native dividers do not need assignees. Subtasks have their own assignees; setting the main-task assignee does not assign its children. Check relevant field availability separately from project membership. Official help has contained conflicting first-level custom-field inheritance wording, so inspect the actual child and intended report rather than guessing.

If a subtask must appear on the project calendar, check its due date, project association, and view filters. Do not create a duplicate merely to make it visible.

Multi-homing means adding the same task to another project. Confirm authorization and destination audience before adding it. The task's shared access can change; a restrictive project does not erase access from other projects. Read back membership and intended visibility.

## Repair existing work

Read all relevant descriptions, comments, subtasks, dependencies, dates, and accepted work first. Preserve IDs and usable history. Identify requested changes and prepare a complete replacement brief before editing active assignments. Explain any required pause. Do not assume changing or removing an assignee is silent.
